passages.t: Everything Jerusalem leans on taken away
passages.happening:
‘For behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts is about to remove from Jerusalem and Judah both supply and support’ (verse 1): food and water, the warrior, the judge and the prophet, the elder, the commander, the counselor and even the magician (verses 1-3). ‘I will make mere lads their leaders, and children will rule over them’ (verse 4).

People will oppress one another, neighbor against neighbor, the young against the old (verse 5). A man will grab his brother and say that since he has a cloak he must be their leader, ruler of a heap of rubble. And the brother will cry out that he is no healer and has nothing in his house, and refuse (verses 6-7).

‘For Jerusalem has stumbled and Judah has fallen because they spoke and acted against the LORD’ (verse 8). Like Sodom they parade their sin (verse 9). ‘Tell the righteous it will be well with them, for they will enjoy the fruit of their labor’ (verse 10). Woe to the wicked, who will be repaid for what their hands have done (verse 11). ‘O My people, your guides mislead you; they turn you from your paths’ (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 2 ended with the warning to stop trusting in man. Chapter 3 shows what happens when God removes the human supports people trust. The list is the ruling class of eighth-century Judah: the warrior, the judge, the prophet, the elder, the commander of fifty. Soothsayers, magicians and enchanters, which Israel's law forbade, are listed among what Jerusalem leaned on, a sign of how far official religion had drifted.

In a society without a state to care for the weak, elders and heads of households held communities together, judged disputes at the gate and protected the vulnerable. When they are gone, everything comes apart. A cloak was a basic possession, and in a ruined city having one was enough to make a man a candidate for leader, though he refuses.

The promise of lads and children as rulers may describe the collapse of competent leadership after war and deportation took the experienced men away, as happened when Babylon later removed Judah's leaders. Some scholars see a pointed reference to a young king, but the text names no one. The collapse came in stages: the Assyrian devastation of 701 BC and, more fully, the Babylonian conquest of 587 or 586 BC.

Verses 10 and 11 interrupt the gloom with a small saying about the righteous and the wicked, which states the moral order beneath the chaos.
passages.later: Jeremiah cries out against the same failure: “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture!” declares the LORD (Jeremiah 23:1). Ezekiel says, ‘Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves’ (Ezekiel 34:2).
passages.asks: God takes away every support Jerusalem leaned on. Ask what you lean on that God could take away, and what would be left. And ask whether you are one of the guides who could mislead others.

passages.t: The LORD's case against the leaders
passages.happening:
‘The LORD arises to contend; He stands to judge the people’ (verse 13).

He brings his charge against the elders and leaders of his people. ‘You have devoured the vineyard; the plunder of the poor is in your houses’ (verse 14). ‘Why do you crush My people and grind the faces of the poor?’ (verse 15), declares the Lord GOD of Hosts.
passages.hearers:
This is a short courtroom scene. The verb to contend, riv, is the verb of a lawsuit, and the LORD rises as prosecutor. The prophets often use it for God's case against his people. It frames the leaders' crimes as breaches of covenant, not only bad policy.

Israel pictured itself as God's vineyard, as chapter 5 will show. To devour the vineyard was to consume the very people the leaders were meant to tend. The plunder of the poor is sitting in their houses. The first hearers could see it: the large houses of the powerful, filled with what had been squeezed from others.

The word for poor, ani, describes people who are powerless and open to abuse. God calls them his own people, and sides with them against their rulers. Grinding the faces of the poor is a picture of crushing people into the dirt.
passages.later: Proverbs gives the same warning: ‘do not crush the afflicted at the gate, for the LORD will take up their case’ (Proverbs 22:22-23). Amos condemns the wealthy of Samaria ‘who oppress the poor and crush the needy’ (Amos 4:1).
passages.asks: God says the plunder of the poor is in the leaders' houses. Ask whether anything in your house came at someone else's expense. And ask who the poor are whose case God would take up against you.

passages.t: The pride of the daughters of Zion undone
passages.happening:
The LORD turns to the wealthy women of Jerusalem. ‘Because the daughters of Zion are haughty’ (verse 16), walking with heads high and roving eyes, mincing along with bracelets jingling on their ankles, the Lord will strike their heads with sores and leave them bare (verse 17).

In that day he will take away their finery: anklets, headbands, crescents, pendants, bracelets, veils, headdresses, sashes, perfume bottles and charms, signet rings and nose rings, festive robes, cloaks, purses, mirrors, linen, tiaras and shawls (verses 18-23).

‘Instead of fragrance there will be a stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of styled hair, baldness; instead of fine clothing, sackcloth; instead of beauty, shame’ (verse 24).

‘Your men will fall by the sword, and your warriors in battle’ (verse 25). The gates of Zion will lament and mourn, and the city, stripped bare, will sit on the ground (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
The list of ornaments in verses 18 to 23 is the longest list of women's clothing and jewelry in the Bible. Several of its Hebrew words occur nowhere else, so some translations are informed guesses, but archaeologists have recovered many such items from the region: crescent-shaped pendants, anklets, nose rings, signet rings, perfume flasks and small amulets. Some had religious or protective meaning as charms. Mirrors were polished bronze.

The indictment is aimed at the wealthy class of Jerusalem, whose luxury was bought with the plunder of the poor that the previous verses described. The men of that class have just been charged. Both are judged for the same sin.

The reversals of verse 24 describe captives being led away: conquerors stripped, bound and sometimes shaved their prisoners. The chapter ends with the city itself pictured as a woman sitting on the ground in mourning, as her men fall in battle.
passages.later: Peter tells believers that beauty ‘should not come from outward adornment’ but from ‘the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit’ (1 Peter 3:3-4). And Lamentations later pictures the same city mourning after the fall, with the elders of Zion who ‘sit on the ground in silence’ (Lamentations 2:10).
passages.hard:
Why are the women of Jerusalem singled out, and why is women ruling named as a judgment (verse 12)?

The passage reflects the social order of Isaiah's day, in which rule by the young and by women was unusual. Its point in verse 12 is that the normal order of society had collapsed, not a general statement about what women can do. The Greek translation and some modern scholars read the Hebrew word in verse 12 with different vowels, as creditors or extortioners rather than women, which would change the line; the Hebrew text as it stands reads women.

The charge against the daughters of Zion is not about women as such but about the wealthy of the city, whose luxury came from plundering the poor. The men of the same class have just been charged with the same sin, and the whole city, men and women, suffers together.

The pictures of verses 17 and 24 describe what conquest did to captives. They are a prophetic picture of a city and its fall. They give no warrant to any man to shame or harm a woman.

If someone is hurting you, at home, at work or in a church, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The women's finery was bought with the plunder of the poor. Ask what your own comforts cost others. And ask what you would grieve if everything you dress yourself in were taken away.
